Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Core Concepts
What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
Retrieval-augmented generation, commonly abbreviated as RAG, is an architecture that combines a
retrieval system with a text generation model. Instead of relying solely on knowledge encoded in a
model's parameters during training, a RAG system fetches relevant documents from an external
knowledge base at query time and provides them to the generation model as context. This grounds
the model's answers in retrievable, verifiable source material and reduces the model's reliance on
potentially outdated or incomplete internal knowledge.
Why Vector Embeddings Instead of Keyword Search?
Traditional keyword search matches exact terms between a query and a document. RAG systems
typically use vector embeddings instead: text is converted into a numerical vector that captures its
semantic meaning. Because embeddings capture meaning rather than exact wording, the system can
find passages that are conceptually related to a query even when they do not share exact keywords.
This significantly improves recall on paraphrased, indirectly worded, or synonym-heavy questions
compared to keyword-only approaches.
The Role of the Vector Store
A vector store is a specialized database that indexes document chunks as embeddings and enables
fast similarity search over them. When a query arrives, it is embedded using the same model used for
the documents, and the vector store returns the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the query
embedding. These top-ranked chunks are then passed to the generation model as context so it can
compose an answer grounded in that retrieved material.
Document Chunking
Chunking is the process of splitting large documents into smaller, more manageable pieces before
they are embedded and indexed. Chunking matters for two reasons. First, it improves retrieval
precision, since a smaller chunk that closely matches a query is more likely to be ranked highly than
an entire, only-partially-relevant document. Second, it respects the generation model's context
window: passing a handful of tightly relevant chunks uses that limited space far more efficiently than
passing whole documents.
Hallucination in RAG SystemsHallucination is a failure mode in which the generation model produces information that sounds
plausible but is not actually supported by the retrieved context or any reliable source. RAG is intended
to reduce hallucination by grounding answers in retrieved evidence, but hallucination can still occur if
the model ignores the provided context, extrapolates beyond it, or if the retriever failed to surface the
necessary information in the first place.
The Retrieval Precision/Recall Tradeoff
Increasing the number of chunks retrieved for a given query can improve recall, since there is a
higher chance that the information needed to answer the question is included somewhere in the
retrieved set. However, retrieving more chunks can also reduce precision, since irrelevant or loosely
related chunks are more likely to be included as noise. This noise can confuse the generation model
or dilute the truly relevant context, so the number of retrieved chunks is a tuning parameter that must
balance recall against precision for a given use case.
Evaluating RAG Systems with RAGAS
RAGAS is an evaluation framework that scores a RAG pipeline using several complementary metrics.
Faithfulness measures whether the claims made in a generated answer are actually supported by the
retrieved context, penalizing unsupported or fabricated claims. Answer relevancy measures how well
the generated answer addresses the specific question asked, penalizing incomplete or off-topic
responses. Context recall measures how much of the information needed to produce the ground-truth
answer was actually present in the retrieved context, indicating whether the retriever fetched enough
relevant material. Context precision measures whether the relevant chunks within the retrieved
context are ranked ahead of irrelevant ones, reflecting how well the retriever prioritizes useful
information over noise.
